segs.text: Module six, objective one. Superposition, and why repeated doses build up. The dosing interval, tau, is the time between doses, so three times a day is a tau of eight hours. The peak is the highest plasma concentration, C p, in an interval, and the trough is the lowest, just before the next dose. Given at a fixed interval, each dose adds to what is left of the earlier ones, so the peaks and troughs climb to a plateau called steady state, marked by an infinity sign. First order elimination removes a fixed fraction of the drug present per unit of time, set by the rate constant k.

card.m: τ: the time between doses, hr; TID → τ = 8 hr
peak = highest C<sub>p</sub> in an interval; trough = lowest, just before the next dose
each dose adds to the leftover → climb → steady state (∞)
first order: a fixed fraction of the drug present removed per hr; k in hr<sup>−1</sup>

segs.text: Drug builds up when the next dose comes before the last one is completely eliminated; with an interval long enough for each dose to be completely eliminated, nothing is left over and nothing builds up. The climb stops because, with first order elimination, the fraction removed per interval stays the same while the amount removed grows with the amount in the body. When the amount removed over one interval equals one dose, every interval repeats. For I V bolus doses the peak minus the trough is then one dose: in amount, the dose itself, and in milligrams per liter, C zero, the concentration one dose produces on its own.

card.m: next dose before the last is eliminated → leftover + new dose → higher peak
interval longer than the time to eliminate a dose → no build-up
per interval: fraction removed constant; amount removed grows with the amount present
amount removed per τ = one dose → steady state
IV bolus at steady state: D<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup> − D<sub>min</sub><sup>∞</sup> = D<sub>0</sub>; C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup> − C<sub>min</sub><sup>∞</sup> = C<sub>0</sub>

segs.text: Steady state takes three to five half lives, the half life being the time for the level to fall by half. That time depends on the half life only: after n doses the level has reached one minus e to the minus n k tau of its plateau, which holds only k and n times tau, the length of n dosing intervals, and no dose. A larger dose raises the plateau in proportion but does not move the time. She said, not three to five doses, three to five half lives. After the last dose, most of the drug is gone in another three to five half lives.

card.m: steady state: 3 to 5 t<sub>½</sub>
fraction of the plateau after n doses = 1 − e<sup>−nkτ</sup>; nτ = n intervals (hr); no D<sub>0</sub>
dose × 2: plateau × 2, same time
after the last dose: most gone in 3 to 5 t<sub>½</sub>

segs.text: Superposition says C p at any time is the sum of what is left of every dose given so far, each following its own single dose curve. It assumes first order elimination, and pharmacokinetics after one dose that are not altered by later doses, so the half life and the clearance, the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit of time, stay the same. Then each dose loses the same fraction per hour whatever else is present, so each leftover can be worked out on its own and the leftovers add. Saturation of a carrier, enzyme induction or inhibition, or a changing disease state break superposition. She said, First order kinetics equals linear pharmacokinetics.

card.m: C<sub>p</sub> = the sum of what is left of each dose
assumes: 1. first-order elimination; 2. t<sub>½</sub> and Cl unchanged by later doses
same fraction lost per hr → each leftover on its own → leftovers add
fails: carrier saturation, induction or inhibition, changing pathophysiology
first order = linear

segs.text: In symbols, C equals C zero e to the minus k t applies after every dose, at steady state as after the first; only the starting value is higher. With t equal to tau, e to the minus k tau is the fraction of a dose left one interval later. The accumulation factor, r, one over one minus e to the minus k tau, is the steady state peak divided by the first dose peak. A shorter tau leaves more behind, so one minus e to the minus k tau, under the one, is smaller and r is larger. The dose is not in r, so doubling the dose doubles every level but leaves r unchanged.

card.m: C = C<sub>0</sub>e<sup>−kt</sup> after every dose
t = τ: e<sup>−kτ</sup> = fraction left after one interval
r = {{frac:1|1 − e<sup>−kτ</sup>}} = {{frac:C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup>|C<sub>0</sub>}}
τ shorter → e<sup>−kτ</sup> larger → 1 − e<sup>−kτ</sup> smaller → r larger
no D<sub>0</sub> in r: dose × 2, levels × 2, r unchanged

segs.text: Since each dose follows the same curve, the area under the curve, A U C, of the first dose from zero to infinity equals the area of one interval at steady state. The average at steady state is that one interval area divided by tau, in milligrams per liter. This area form is not on the equation sheet.

card.m: [AUC]<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> of dose 1 = [AUC]<sub>t1</sub><sup>t2</sup> of one interval at steady state
C<sub>av</sub><sup>∞</sup> = {{frac:[AUC]<sub>t1</sub><sup>t2</sup>|τ}}: {{frac:mg hr/L|hr}} = mg/L
not on the sheet

segs.text: For her Example one regimen, a half life of four hours, a volume of distribution of zero point two five liters per kilogram, and ten milligrams per kilogram by I V bolus every eight hours, find the peak after the second dose and the time to steady state. By superposition, the second peak is the second dose's forty plus the ten milligrams per liter left of the first after eight hours, two half lives: fifty milligrams per liter. Steady state comes in three to five half lives, twelve to twenty hours. At steady state the peak is one dose's forty plus the trough, a quarter of the peak, so forty is three quarters of the peak: fifty three point three milligrams per liter, and the trough is thirteen point three.

card.m: t<sub>½</sub> = 4 hr, V<sub>D</sub> = 0.25 L/kg, 10 mg/kg IV bolus every 8 hr
C<sub>0</sub> = {{frac:10 mg/kg|0.25 L/kg}} = 40 mg/L; 8 hr = 2 t<sub>½</sub>: 40 → 20 → 10 mg/L
3 × 4 hr = 12 hr to 5 × 4 hr = 20 hr: steady state within 12 to 20 hr
{{frac:53.3|40}} = 1.33 = r for τ = 2 t<sub>½</sub>

segs.text: Her items test the wording. Of the two assumptions of superposition, the second is the one that names the half life and the clearance, and a review item states it as early doses having no effect on the pharmacokinetics of later doses, which is true. Steady state takes three to five half lives, not three to five doses, and does not depend on the dose. e to the minus k tau is the fraction of one dose left after one interval, while the accumulation factor is the steady state peak divided by the first dose peak. First order and linear mean the same, and objectives two and three build on superposition.

card.m: ✓ early doses do not change the PK of later doses (True)
✓ 3 to 5 t<sub>½</sub>; not 3 to 5 doses; not dose-dependent
e<sup>−kτ</sup>: left after one τ; r = {{frac:C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup>|C<sub>0</sub>}}
first order = linear
